title: Twenty-Four Jams or Six
text:
On two Saturdays at Draeger's, an upscale supermarket in Menlo Park, California, the psychologists Sheena Iyengar and Mark Lepper set up a tasting booth for a brand of jam. Through the day they switched the display back and forth. Sometimes it offered 24 flavors; sometimes only 6. Shoppers who stopped received a discount coupon for any jar of that brand.

The large display drew more attention: about 60 percent of passing shoppers stopped at it, against about 40 percent for the small one. But buying told a different story. Only about 3 percent of the people who stopped at the 24-jam table later bought a jar, while about 30 percent of those who saw just 6 flavors did.

In other studies in the same paper, students who chose from a small set of chocolates were more satisfied with their pick than those who chose from a large set, and students given a short list of essay topics were more likely to write the essay.

Published in 2000, the jam study became a famous example of choice overload: too many options can make people freeze or feel worse about what they pick. Later research was more cautious. A 2010 meta-analysis by Benjamin Scheibehenne and colleagues found that the average effect across many studies was close to zero, with overload appearing only under certain conditions, such as when options are hard to compare or people have no clear preferences.
lesson: When you offer choices, to customers, colleagues or yourself, make them easy to compare. If the options are many and similar, narrowing them down first can help people actually decide.
location: Draeger's supermarket, Menlo Park, California, USA
source: Iyengar, S. S., and Lepper, M. R. (2000). When choice is demotivating: Can one desire too much of a good thing? Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 79(6), 995-1006.
caveat: A 2010 meta-analysis (Scheibehenne, Greifeneder and Todd) found the average choice overload effect near zero, so it appears only under specific conditions.
